# Summary {.unnumbered}

**Aim.** Bulk pancreatic tumors mix tumor, stromal and immune signals. We ask whether a Bayesian
matrix factorization that lets survival inform its molecular programs can find prognostic
programs that an unsupervised factorization misses, and whether its risk score transfers to new
cohorts.

**Method.** The model factorizes expression into patient activities and gene loadings and links
survival through a Cox model on the projection of each patient's expression onto the loadings.
A survival weight $w_S$ sets how much the Cox partial likelihood is weighted relative to the expression
likelihood. The primary comparator uses the same factorization at the same rank fitted without
survival, followed by a Cox model on its program scores.

**Results.** The working model is the supervised YFB fit ($w_S = 1$, 2,218 genes, rank
`r tcv_K`). On the `r train_n[["TCGA_PAAD"]] + train_n[["CPTAC"]]` training patients its
five-fold cross-validated concordance within cohort was `r num(k5_cw$mean_YFB)` (SE
`r num(k5_se_y)`), and every fold fit converged. Scored once on `r nrow(e_w1)` external series,
its mean concordance was `r num(kp("equal_YFB")$estimate)` (95% donor-bootstrap interval
`r ci(kp("equal_YFB")$lower, kp("equal_YFB")$upper)`), and `r length(k5_active)` of its
`r tcv_K` programs were survival-active (@sec-working-model). The supervised and two-step fits
had small estimated performance differences (@sec-results-fair). Counting all pairs in each held-out fold, their mean
fold concordances were `r num(cv_w1$mean_C)` and
`r num(cv_ts$mean_C)`, a paired difference of `r sgn(cv_diff)` (SE `r num(cv_diff_se)`), and
their mean external concordances were `r num(mean(e_w1$C))` and `r num(mean(e_ts$C))`, a pooled
paired difference of `r sgn(pool5$diff)` (95% donor-bootstrap interval
`r ci(pool_donor$lo, pool_donor$hi)`). The largest median survival share of
loading precision across programs, gene-set sizes and fits was `r sci(share_rng[2])`, and the supervised and unsupervised loadings correlate at 1.000. Against
DeSurv, elastic-net Cox and PurIST, all trained on the same patients, every paired difference
in mean external concordance had a 95% interval that included zero
(@sec-results-comparators). In simulations fitted at rank 7, supervision matches the two-step fit
when a prognostic program is easy to find, and it improved recovery near the detection
threshold under strong survival. Choosing the weight by cross-validated partial log-likelihood
on the training data kept $w_S = 1$. The fit is not pruned, because ELBO pruning lost the
planted program in simulation, and its rank comes from training cross-validation.

**External cohorts.** Under the current rule, modeling choices are made by simulation and five-fold
cross-validation on the `r train_n[["TCGA_PAAD"]] + train_n[["CPTAC"]]` TCGA and CPTAC training
patients. This covers preprocessing, gene screening, priors, rank, survival weight and
comparator tuning. The five external expression series and the matched ICGC methylation set
only score a model that is already fixed. Earlier development used external concordance
to choose the screen and scaling, to pool the training cohorts without a cohort indicator and
to constrain the starting values, so these series are not untouched validation data
(@sec-external-uses). Training cross-validation kept the gene screen and
the per-cohort standardization and selected rank `r tcv_K` for the working model
(@sec-results-rank).

**Work of November 9–13.** The analyses of this week compare priors on the loadings and the
survival coefficients, fit methylation alone, test one fitter for several data types, compare
two ways of linking survival to the programs, and reselect the gene screen, input scaling and
rank on training data.
The current
model keeps point-Laplace priors on the scores and loadings and a Normal prior on each survival
coefficient ([Appendix D](#sec-appendix-d)). It also keeps the gene screen and the z-scores
within cohort, and the one-standard-error rule selects rank `r tcv_K` (@sec-results-rank). At
rank `r tcv_K` the projection and latent-score models had small paired differences in
training and external concordance, and the projection model is kept (@sec-week-lb). Methylation alone,
on `r meth_aud$n` matched TCGA patients, had mean cross-validated concordance of
`r num(min(meth_ok$mean_C), 2)` to `r num(max(meth_ok$mean_C), 2)`, close to 0.5. It was below
expression on the same patients in all `r nrow(meth_ok1)` comparisons, but only
`r sum(meth_zd > 2)` differences exceeded two paired standard errors. It found no
survival-active program that the expression fit lacks. Its
programs share two strong directions with the expression programs, and a few recurring
programs are specific to methylation (@sec-week-methylation). Preliminary results for the feature-group fitter and its descriptive matched-TCGA comparison are reported in @sec-week-multimodal.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Notation {#sec-notation}

Patients are indexed by $i = 1, \dots, n$, genes by $j = 1, \dots, p$ and programs (factors) by
$k = 1, \dots, K$. Patient $i$ has observed time $t_i$ and event indicator $\delta_i$ (1 for
death, 0 for censoring). The training data are an $n \times p$ expression matrix $Y$. For a
random quantity $\theta$ under the variational posterior $q$, $\bar\theta = E_q\theta$.

Two patient-level quantities are kept apart. The **activities** $L \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times K}$
are posterior scores in the reconstruction $Y \approx LF^\top$ and exist only for training
patients. The **program scores** $Z = Y\bar F$ are the product of a patient's expression with
the posterior-mean loadings. They enter the Cox predictor and can be computed for any new
patient whose expression is measured on the same genes.

## Model {#sec-model}

The expression matrix is modeled as
$$
y_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K L_{ik} F_{jk} + e_{ij}, \qquad e_{ij} \sim N(0, \tau_j^{-1}),
$$ {#eq-recon}
with independent point-Laplace priors on the entries of each column of $L$ and $F$, a point mass
at zero mixed with a Laplace distribution, whose parameters are estimated by empirical Bayes
within each program with the R package ebnm [@Willwerscheid2025]. Each gene has its own residual
precision $\tau_j$. Survival follows a Cox model [@Cox1972] whose linear predictor is the
program-score projection,
$$
\eta_i = \sum_{k=1}^K Z_{ik}\beta_k, \qquad Z = Y\bar F, \qquad \beta_k \sim N(0, \sigma_k^2),
$$ {#eq-eta}
with the prior variance $\sigma_k^2$ estimated per program. This is the YFB model, named for its
predictor $\eta = (YF)\beta$. Because new patients are scored by the same projection, prediction
needs no refitting.

The variational objective is
$$
E_q \log p(Y \mid L, F, \tau) \;+\; w_S\, E_q \log \mathrm{PL}(\beta, F) \;-\; \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, \text{prior}),
$$ {#eq-objective}
where $\mathrm{PL}$ is the Cox partial likelihood. The survival weight $w_S$ multiplies the Cox
term wherever it appears: in the loading update, in the coefficient update and in the objective.
At $w_S = 1$ the objective is the evidence lower bound of the joint model. Larger values of $w_S$
give survival more influence on the loadings. The full derivation, with every update checked
term by term against the code, is in
`derivations/SSBMF-YFB-model-derivations/SSBMF-YFB-model-derivation-full.pdf` (Appendix A).

**Scale.** The reconstruction does not fix the scale of a program: multiplying $L_{\cdot k}$ by
$c$ and dividing $F_{\cdot k}$ by $c$ leaves $LF^\top$ unchanged. The fit therefore rescales
each nonzero program after a sweep so that its posterior mean training projection has standard deviation 1. Each
$\beta_k$ is then a log hazard ratio per standard deviation of the program score, and a single
$w_S$ means the same thing for every program.

## Fitting and prediction {#sec-fitting}

Each sweep re-expands the Cox partial likelihood to second order around the current
$\bar\eta$, with the predictor's variance taken from $q(\beta)$ and $q(F)$. It then updates, one
program at a time, the coefficient, the activities and the loadings. The loading update uses the reconstruction residual and the weighted Cox contribution to its precision and linear term. Each sweep ends by updating the noise precisions and rescaling the programs. The fit starts from the
singular value decomposition of $Y$ and stops when the relative change in the objective falls
below $10^{-5}$ or after 300 sweeps. The working fit is not pruned (@sec-results-pruning) and has rank `r tcv_K` (@sec-results-rank).

New cohorts are standardized gene by gene within cohort and scored on the training genes they
measure. The direction of the risk score is the one the fit learns from training survival. There
is no post-fit sign correction: a fit oriented the wrong way would have training concordance
below 0.5 and is reported as fitted.

## The two-step comparator {#sec-two-step}

The rank-matched comparison uses the same fitter at $w_S = 0$, which
removes survival from the loading update and gives the unsupervised empirical-Bayes
factorization at the same rank, on the same genes and patients. Because $w_S$ also multiplies the
Cox term in the coefficient update, $w_S = 0$ gives $\beta = 0$. The two-step comparator
therefore takes the $w_S = 0$ loadings and fits an unpenalized Cox model on the training program
scores. It differs from the supervised fit only in whether survival entered the loadings and in
how $\beta$ was estimated.

## Choosing the survival weight {#sec-weight}

The real-data fit uses $w_S = 1$, fixed by five-fold training cross-validation
(@sec-results-s15). Two refinements were tested in simulation. In the survival-block form,
$w_S$ multiplies the Cox term and the Kullback–Leibler term of $\beta$ together, so $\beta$ gets
an ordinary Bayesian Cox fit while the loadings see survival at weight $w_S$. The weight is
chosen for each dataset from $\{1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50\}$ by five-fold cross-validated partial
log-likelihood, with ties going to the smaller weight. The same rule was applied to the real
training data (@sec-results-s15).

## Choosing the gene screen, input scaling and rank {#sec-rank}

The gene screen and the input scaling were compared with alternatives by five-fold training
cross-validation on the folds of @sec-results-fair, using concordance within cohort. The current
screen is the 2,218-gene set described in @sec-data. The alternative is a different preprocessing configuration, not
only a different ranking rule. It z-scores each cohort, quantile-normalizes the merged matrix and keeps the 2,000 genes of largest variance. Neither
screen uses outcomes, so each was computed once on all training patients, as in DeSurv. The
alternative scalings divide each gene by its within-cohort standard deviation, with the Cox
projection centered, or apply the within-patient rank transform of DeSurv followed by z-scores
within cohort [@Young2026]. The current choice was kept unless an alternative was better by more
than one standard error of the paired fold difference.

The rank is not chosen by ELBO pruning, which lost the planted program in simulation
(@sec-results-pruning). We chose it by five-fold training cross-validation with the
one-standard-error rule. The rule takes the smallest $K$ from 2 to 12 whose mean
concordance is at least the best mean minus the standard error of the fold concordances at the
best $K$. Without pruning the fit keeps every column it starts with, so cross-validation chooses
the fitted rank.

## The models behind the reported results {#sec-model-states}

The working model is the supervised YFB fit ($w_S = 1$, 2,218 genes, rank `r tcv_K`). It is
`fit_ssbmf_yfb(canonicalize = TRUE, w_S = 1)` on the 2,218-gene set, with every RNA-seq cohort
logged once and z-scored gene by gene within cohort, `r tcv_K` programs without pruning,
point-Laplace priors on $L$ and $F$ and a Normal prior on $\beta$. The survival weight, the
gene-set size, the choice not to screen genes on survival, the priors and the rank were fixed by
training cross-validation. The gene screen and the input scaling were first set with external
concordance (@sec-external-uses), and training cross-validation has since kept both
(@sec-results-rank). External concordance also informed two earlier choices: pooling the
training cohorts without a cohort indicator and the constraints on the singular value
decomposition used to start the fit. Its training cross-validation, survival-active programs and external
concordance are reported in @sec-working-model.

Every result for the real data comes from this fit, except the comparison of the gene screen and input scaling (@tbl-inputs) and the
prior comparisons ([Appendix D](#sec-appendix-d)). These use the rank-7 reference, the same
supervised YFB configuration ($w_S = 1$, 2,218 genes) fitted at rank 7, and say so. The five
programs of the rank-`r tcv_K` fit match Programs 1 to 5 of the rank-7 reference one to one
(@tbl-correspondence in Appendix C). Rank-7 Programs 6 and 7 have no rank-`r tcv_K` counterpart, and neither
was survival-active.


# Evaluation {#sec-evaluation}

## Data {#sec-data}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cohorts
#| tbl-cap: "Training and validation cohorts. Patient and death counts are read from the saved fold table and external scoring results. Scores omit training genes absent from the external series. PACA-AU is the Australian pancreatic cancer project of the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC). Its array and RNA-seq series share donors. TCGA-PAAD, The Cancer Genome Atlas pancreatic adenocarcinoma cohort. CPTAC, Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium. RNA-seq, RNA sequencing."
tab <- rbind(
  data.frame(Cohort = c("TCGA-PAAD", "CPTAC"), Platform = "RNA-seq",
             Patients = as.integer(train_n[c("TCGA_PAAD", "CPTAC")]),
             Deaths = as.integer(train_d[c("TCGA_PAAD", "CPTAC")]),
             `Missing genes` = 0L, Role = "Training", check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Cohort = cohort_label[e_w1$cohort], Platform = cohort_platform[e_w1$cohort],
             Patients = e_w1$n, Deaths = e_w1$events, `Missing genes` = e_w1$missing_genes,
             Role = "External validation", check.names = FALSE))
kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The model is trained on `r train_n[["TCGA_PAAD"]] + train_n[["CPTAC"]]` patients
(`r train_d[["TCGA_PAAD"]] + train_d[["CPTAC"]]` deaths) from two RNA-seq cohorts, TCGA-PAAD and
CPTAC (@tbl-cohorts). Every RNA-seq cohort is transformed once by $\log_2(x+1)$. Genes are
screened separately in each training cohort by the combined mean and variance rank of DeSurv
[@Young2026], keeping the top 3,000 per cohort. The screen uses no outcomes. The intersection,
called the 2,218-gene set, has `r big(genes$n_genes[genes$arm == "single"])` genes. Each cohort
is then standardized gene by gene to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The `r nrow(e_w1)` external series supply `r big(ext_records)` records and `r big(ext_deaths)` recorded deaths. The PACA-AU array and RNA-seq series share `r donors$shared_donors` donors,
and the RNA-seq series has `r donors$seq_records` records from `r donors$seq_donors` donors,
so the external collection represents `r ext_people`
people if the other cohorts are distinct (counts from the October 16 accuracy review,
`paper/writeup/2026-10-16-writeup/_process/Accuracy_Review_Dispositions_10_16_26.md`).

## Uses of the external cohorts {#sec-external-uses}

The current selection rule uses simulation and five-fold cross-validation on the
`r train_n[["TCGA_PAAD"]] + train_n[["CPTAC"]]` TCGA and CPTAC training patients. This includes
preprocessing, gene screening, the priors, the rank, the survival weight and the tuning of
comparators. The five external expression series (Dijk, Moffitt, PACA-AU array, PACA-AU RNA-seq
and Puleo) and the matched ICGC methylation set only score a model after it is fixed. Under this rule, their
results are reported and do not choose between models or settings. The DeSurv comparator
used its published settings rather than a new search on our folds. Four choices were made
before this rule with external concordance among the evidence: the gene screen, the
per-cohort standardization without a rank transform, pooling the training cohorts without a
cohort indicator and the constraints on the singular value decomposition that starts the fit.
Training cross-validation has since kept the screen and the standardization and selected rank
`r tcv_K` (@sec-rank, @sec-results-rank). The audit in
`docs/findings/2026-11-06-external-cohort-uses.md` records which earlier choices used which
series. It also notes that the matched ICGC methylation set overlaps the PACA-AU donors and
has been examined in earlier analyses.

The rule follows the protocol DeSurv used on the same cohorts [@Young2026]. DeSurv was trained on
TCGA and CPTAC pooled. Every hyperparameter was chosen by five-fold cross-validation on the
training data, with the one-standard-error rule for the rank, and the external cohorts were
scored once with the final model. No portion of the training data is held out here either.
With 273 patients, a held-out fifth would estimate concordance with a standard error near
0.05, larger than the differences between the settings being compared.

## Simulation designs {#sec-sim-designs}

All three simulation studies plant a single prognostic program among unsupervised structure and
ask whether the fit recovers it. All three fit rank 7, as do the permuted-survival and
mixed-signal simulations of @sec-results. Recovery requires absolute loading correlation of at least 0.7, an active coefficient and the correct coefficient sign after loading alignment. A **false-active** program is one
whose coefficient lies more than 1.96 posterior standard deviations from zero but which does not
match the planted program.

- **The fixed-weight simulation.** Survival weight at 2,000 genes. Data with `r paste(big(sort(unique(s9_design$p))), collapse = " or ")` genes and a planted program
  explaining `r paste(pct(sort(unique(s9_design$variance)), 2), collapse = ", ")` of expression
  variance. We fitted `r length(unique(s9_design$seed))` datasets per cell at
  $w_S \in \{0, 1, 10, 100, 1{,}000, 10{,}000\}$, at $w_S = p/50$ and at a weight calibrated to give
  survival 20% of the loading precision. The generator uses strong planted survival effects.
- **The cross-validated-weight simulation.** The larger gene-count cells of the fixed-weight simulation plus a cell with
  weaker survival. The weight was chosen per dataset by the rule of @sec-weight. Two fits differ in the coefficient posterior. The block-weighted fit uses a mean-field posterior, with the survival weight multiplying the Cox term and the Kullback–Leibler term of $\beta$. The joint-posterior fit is block-weighted with a joint Gaussian
  posterior for $\beta$.
- **The near-threshold simulation.** Programs near the detection threshold. Planted programs explained `r paste(pct(s14_shares, 2), collapse = ", ")`
  of expression variance, with `r s14_n` datasets per cell. The mean oracle concordance ranges
  were `r s14_oracle_ranges[["strong"]]` for strong survival and
  `r s14_oracle_ranges[["realistic"]]` for realistic survival.

The cross-validated-weight and near-threshold simulations compare the supervised and matched two-step fits on the same datasets. The unsupervised reference in the fixed-weight simulation was uncentered, so the matched two-step comparison on its cells comes from the cross-validated-weight simulation.

## Performance metrics and uncertainty {#sec-metrics}

Discrimination is Harrell's concordance index C [@Harrell1982], with the risk direction fixed
from training. Paired differences between two models use percentile bootstrap intervals
[@EfronTibshirani1993] from resampling patients within each cohort, with both models scored on
the same resamples. The pooled difference is the equal-weight mean of the within-series differences. Calibration is the slope from a Cox regression of held-out survival on the fitted score. A slope above one indicates fitted risk differences that are too small. A slope below one indicates differences that are too large. In simulation the slopes use exact event times, because
the default tie handling of `survival::coxph()` merges the extreme simulated times and flattens
every slope.

The record bootstrap resamples records within series. The donor sensitivity
resamples each donor together with every observed record, so the `r donors$shared_donors`
donors shared by the two PACA-AU series move together. Both pooled intervals use the same
equal-weight mean of the within-series differences.

# Work of November 9–13 {#sec-week}

This section reports the analyses of the week of November 9. Unless a subsection says otherwise,
the simulation cells are the three planted variance shares of the fixed-weight simulation
(0.25%, 1% and 5% at 2,000 genes) and the near-threshold cell with a 0.05% share and strong
survival. The real-data comparisons use the five training folds of @sec-results-fair, balanced
by cohort and event. The prior comparisons use the rank-7 reference (@sec-model-states), and
the comparison of the two survival links and the methylation fits use rank `r tcv_K`. All fits
use the unit survival weight unless the subsection varies it. None of these analyses uses an
external cohort to make a choice.

## Priors on the scores and loadings {#sec-week-lf}

A nonnegative factorization, as in DeSurv, makes each program an additive set of genes. This
comparison asks whether point-exponential priors on $L$ and $F$
recover a planted prognostic program as well as the working point-Laplace fit, with false
activity and convergence under control, and whether they predict as well under training
cross-validation. The point-exponential fit takes nonnegative input, each gene divided by its
within-cohort standard deviation without centering, and centers the program scores that enter
the Cox model. The point-Laplace fit takes the working z-scored input. Both arms are fitted to
the pooled training data without cohort strata. Within-cohort concordance is the primary
cross-validation metric, with pooled concordance reported beside it.

**Result.** The point-Laplace prior on z-scores within cohort is kept. In simulation the
point-exponential prior recovered the planted program at least as often. It also marked more
programs survival-active that matched no planted program in the three variance cells
(`r num(min(lf_pe$mean_false_active[-1]), 1)` to `r num(max(lf_pe$mean_false_active[-1]), 1)` per fit
against `r num(min(lf_pl$mean_false_active[-1]), 1)` to `r num(max(lf_pl$mean_false_active[-1]), 1)`),
though fewer at the `r cell_share[[1]]` share (`r num(lf_pe$mean_false_active[1], 1)` against
`r num(lf_pl$mean_false_active[1], 1)`). In the shifted-input fits, the only fits where their size
was measured, these programs had small coefficients relative to the planted program's. The difference appeared in training cross-validation, where its within-cohort
concordance was `r num(min(lf_real[pe_alt, "C"]))` to `r num(max(lf_real[pe_alt, "C"]))` across
four input setups, against `r num(lf_real["PL", "C"])` for the rank-7 point-Laplace fit, and no setup
converged in more than `r max(lf_real[pe_alt, "conv"])` of 5 folds. Tables and details are in [Appendix D](#sec-appendix-d).

## Prior on the survival coefficients {#sec-week-beta}

Under the $L$ and $F$ prior chosen above, this comparison asks which prior on $\beta$ the
working model should use: point-Laplace, point-normal or Normal. The working fit has used a
Normal prior without a comparison that chose it. The three arms differ only in
the $\beta$ prior and use the same simulation cells and training folds. For the point-normal
prior the posterior inclusion probability of each program is also recorded.

**Result.** The Normal prior on each coefficient is kept. A shared point-Laplace, a shared
point-normal and a shared Normal prior gave nearly the same fits, with within-cohort
cross-validated concordance from `r num(min(b_C))` to `r num(max(b_C))` across the four priors
and convergence in the same `r unname(b_conv[1])` of 5 folds. Under
the shared point-normal prior the posterior inclusion probabilities of the full training fit
were `r num(min(b_pip_full$pip), 2)` to `r num(max(b_pip_full$pip), 2)` for all seven programs,
so they do not single out the `r length(b_active_full)` survival-active programs
([Appendix D](#sec-appendix-d)).

## Methylation fitted alone {#sec-week-methylation}

This analysis asks whether the single-modality model, fitted to methylation alone, finds
prognostic programs that the expression fit does not. It uses the `r meth_aud$n` matched TCGA
patients with expression, methylation and survival (`r meth_aud$events` deaths), split into five
folds balanced by event. CpGs with mean methylated fraction between 0.1 and 0.9 on these
patients (`r big(meth_cpg)` CpGs) are ranked by variance, and the fit is run on the top 10,000,
25,000, 50,000 and 100,000 and on all of them. Two setups are fitted at rank `r tcv_K` with a
Normal prior on $\beta$. The first z-scores each CpG and uses point-Laplace priors on $L$ and
$F$, as in the working model. The second divides each CpG by its standard deviation and uses
point-exponential priors with a centered Cox projection, as in @sec-week-lf. The comparison is
with an expression fit on the 2,218 genes for the same patients, folds and setup. We looked
for methylation programs whose patient scores correlate below 0.5 with every expression program
score and that are survival-active in the full fit and in at least three of five folds. A full fit at each count is run first, and cross-validation runs only for counts and
setups whose full fit converges. CpG screening and imputation of missing values used all
`r meth_aud$n` patients before the folds were split, so the held-out patients helped choose the
CpGs. Neither step uses outcomes. With `r meth_aud$n` patients the comparison is descriptive.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-methylation
#| tbl-cap: "Methylation alone at rank 5 on the matched TCGA patients, five-fold cross-validation. The expression row of each setup uses the 2,218 genes on the same patients and folds. Full fit gives whether the fit to all patients converged, with its number of sweeps. Methylation fits stopped at 300 sweeps and expression fits at 1,000. The eight expression fits that reached 300 sweeps were rerun to a 1,000-sweep limit. Capped methylation fits were not rerun. These are the point-exponential full fits at 10,000, 25,000 and 50,000 CpGs and one point-exponential fold at 100,000 CpGs, whose capped state is included in that row's mean. For methylation, cross-validation was run only when the full fit converged. Concordance counts all pairs of these patients. The difference is methylation minus expression in the same setup, paired over folds, with its standard error."
setup_lab <- c(PL = "z-scores, point-Laplace", PE = "Divided by SD, point-exponential")
mf <- meth_full[order(match(meth_full$arm, names(setup_lab)), meth_full$modality != "expression", meth_full$count), ]
mc <- meth_cv1k[match(paste(mf$arm, mf$count), paste(meth_cv1k$arm, meth_cv1k$count)), ]
mx <- subset(meth_x1k, fold == 0)[match(mf$arm, subset(meth_x1k, fold == 0)$arm), ]
is_ex <- mf$modality == "expression"
kable(data.frame(Setup = unname(setup_lab[mf$arm]),
  Data = ifelse(is_ex, "Expression, 2,218 genes", paste0("Methylation, ", big(mf$count), " CpGs")),
  `Full fit` = ifelse(is_ex, paste0("Converged (", mx$iterations, ")"),
                      paste0(ifelse(mf$converged, "Converged", "Reached cap"), " (", mf$iterations, ")")),
  `Folds converged` = ifelse(is_ex, "5/5",
                             ifelse(is.na(mc$methylation_mean_C), "Not run",
                                    paste0(meth_cv$converged_folds[match(paste(mf$arm, mf$count), paste(meth_cv$arm, meth_cv$count))], "/5"))),
  `Mean C` = ifelse(is_ex, num(meth_xC[mf$arm]), ifelse(is.na(mc$methylation_mean_C), "", num(mc$methylation_mean_C))),
  `Difference (SE)` = ifelse(is_ex | is.na(mc$methylation_mean_C), "",
                             paste0(sgn(mc$mean_difference_1000), " (", num(mc$paired_SE_1000), ")")),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "llcccc")
```

**Result.** Methylation alone had concordance close to 0.5 and below expression on the same
patients in every comparison, though most differences were within two paired standard errors.
It found no survival-active program that the expression fit lacks (@tbl-methylation). All `r nrow(meth_all)` fits ran without errors or warnings. The
`r nrow(meth_rr)` expression fits that stopped at 300 sweeps were restarted from the same
initialization with a 1,000-sweep limit. All converged, in `r min(meth_rr$iterations)` to
`r max(meth_rr$iterations)` sweeps, and reproduced their first 300 ELBO values exactly, so
every expression fit now converges. The point-exponential methylation full fits reached the
300-sweep cap at `r paste(paste(big(sort(meth_pe_capped))[-length(meth_pe_capped)], collapse = ", "), "and", big(max(meth_pe_capped)))` CpGs, so those counts were not
cross-validated, and `r sum(meth_cvm$converged)` of the `r nrow(meth_cvm)` methylation fold fits
converged. The capped methylation fits were not rerun with a higher limit. The one capped fold
is a point-exponential fold at `r big(meth_capped_fold$count)` CpGs, and the mean of
`r num(meth_ok$mean_C[meth_ok$arm == "PE" & meth_ok$count == meth_capped_fold$count])` for that
setting includes it. A full fit took `r num(min(meth_min("PL")), 1)` to `r num(max(meth_min("PL")), 1)`
minutes with the point-Laplace setup and `r num(min(meth_min("PE")), 1)` to
`r num(max(meth_min("PE")), 1)` minutes with the point-exponential setup, growing with the
number of CpGs.

Mean cross-validated concordance of methylation alone was `r num(min(meth_ok$mean_C))` to
`r num(max(meth_ok$mean_C))` across counts and setups, against `r num(meth_xC[["PL"]])` for
expression with the point-Laplace setup and `r num(meth_xC[["PE"]])` with the
point-exponential setup. Methylation was below expression in all `r nrow(meth_ok1)`
comparisons, by `r num(min(meth_d("PL")))` to `r num(max(meth_d("PL")))` with the
point-Laplace setup and by `r andj(num(sort(meth_d("PE"))))` with the point-exponential setup.
The paired standard errors were `r num(min(meth_ok1$paired_SE_1000))` to
`r num(max(meth_ok1$paired_SE_1000))`, so the differences were
`r num(min(meth_zd), 1)` to `r num(max(meth_zd), 1)` standard errors, and
`r sum(meth_zd > 2)` of the `r nrow(meth_ok1)` exceeded two. The comparisons within each setup
share one expression reference, so they are not independent. Single methylation folds ranged from
`r num(min(meth_cvm$C), 2)` to `r num(max(meth_cvm$C), 2)`.

Every full fit kept `r tcv_K` programs with nonzero loadings. With the point-Laplace setup the
only survival-active methylation program was Program `r meth_act$program` at
`r big(meth_act$count)` CpGs, with coefficient `r num(meth_act$beta_mean)` (SD
`r num(meth_act$beta_sd)`). It was survival-active in `r meth_act$active_converged_folds` of 5
folds, and its scores correlated `r num(meth_act$max_abs_expression_r)` with an expression
program, so it is not distinct from the expression programs. Neither converged
point-exponential full fit had a survival-active program.

**Methylation programs compared with expression programs.** We then compared the patient
scores of each methylation fit with those of the expression fit in the same setup, without
regard to survival. The two sets of scores share two strong directions. Across the
`r length(unique(paste(meth_cca$arm, meth_cca$count)))` comparisons the first two canonical
correlations were `r num(meth_ccr(1)[1], 2)` to `r num(meth_ccr(1)[2], 2)` and
`r num(meth_ccr(2)[1], 2)` to `r num(meth_ccr(2)[2], 2)`, and the fifth was
`r num(meth_ccr(5)[1], 2)` to `r num(meth_ccr(5)[2], 2)`. We called a methylation program
methylation-specific if its scores correlated below 0.5 with every expression program, it was
matched in at least three folds and it recurred at another CpG count. By this descriptive rule
`r nrow(meth_spec)` of the `r nrow(meth_fst)` program fits were methylation-specific,
`r sum(meth_spec$arm == "PL")` with point-Laplace and `r sum(meth_spec$arm == "PE")` with
point-exponential. These are a few programs seen at several counts, not `r nrow(meth_spec)`
separate programs. Regressing each one on all five expression program scores gave $R^2$ below
0.25 for `r sum(meth_r2s$R2 < 0.25)` of the `r nrow(meth_r2s)`, all at 100,000 or all CpGs,
and above 0.5 for
`r sum(meth_r2s$R2 > 0.5)`, which are mostly combinations of expression programs. The clearest
methylation-specific program is point-Laplace Program 2 at 100,000 and at all CpGs ($R^2$
`r num(meth_clr$R2[meth_clr$count == 100000], 2)` and
`r num(meth_clr$R2[meth_clr$count == meth_cpg], 2)`). At 100,000 CpGs its strongest Hallmark
associations were allograft rejection and TNF-$\alpha$ signaling, which suggests an immune component.
The gene-set analysis covers only the 2,218 genes. The methylation program most related to
purity, point-Laplace Program `r meth_pur_top$factor`, correlated up to
`r num(meth_pur_top$abs_correlation, 2)` in absolute value with ABSOLUTE tumor purity
(`r meth_pur_top$n_complete` of `r meth_aud$n` patients), and its closest expression program
is Program `r unique(meth_fst$closest_expression_factor[meth_fst$arm == meth_pur_top$arm & meth_fst$factor == meth_pur_top$factor])`.

Of the `r big(nrow(meth_pcg))` pairs of a promoter CpG and one of the 2,218 genes,
`r num(100 * mean(meth_pcg$spearman_r < 0), 1)`% had a negative Spearman correlation between
methylation and expression. These correlations are not adjusted for purity. The top 100 CpGs
of a methylation program rarely annotate to the top 100 genes of its closest expression
program (`r min(meth_ovl$observed)` to `r max(meth_ovl$observed)` of 100), and no comparison
was significant after a Bonferroni correction over the `r nrow(meth_ovl)` comparisons.

The 100,000-CpG point-Laplace Program 2 was tracked across CpG counts on the same patients. At 10,000 CpGs its signal was split between Programs 2 and 4, with absolute correlations 0.61 and 0.59. Their $R^2$ values on the five expression programs were 0.52 and 0.43. The five 10,000-CpG programs together explained 80% of the 100,000-CpG program's score variance. At 50,000 CpGs the best single match had absolute correlation 0.89 and $R^2$ 0.25 on expression. The 100,000-CpG and all-CpG matches had $R^2$ 0.06 and 0.04. These in-sample comparisons suggest that 10,000 CpGs already contain methylation information not captured by expression. That information is split across two programs, and both share part of their variation with the expression programs.

We report 10,000 CpGs under point-Laplace for prediction and for the first joint fit, and 100,000 CpGs to describe the methylation-specific program. At 10,000 CpGs the full fit and all five folds converged, the fit already contains the recurring methylation-specific signal, and its methylation cross-validated concordance was the highest of the seven settings. Because it was the best of seven, that concordance is optimistic. The choice was made before any ICGC scoring. The fixed models were later scored once in the matched ICGC set, and those results are in @sec-week-multimodal. With `r meth_aud$n` patients these comparisons are descriptive.

## One fitter for several data types {#sec-week-multimodal}

The results in this section are preliminary. The YFB fitter now accepts feature groups with shared scores $L$ and separate loading priors for each data type. Its single-group path reproduced the existing fitter bit for bit on pooled and stratified-centered test fixtures. Checks also cover the Gaussian activity Kullback–Leibler term, the flat coefficient likelihood, grouped prior updates and the loading divergence under the returned prior.

A two-data-type simulation examined grouped and pooled loading priors. In the informative scenario with equal feature counts and 3% nonzero methylation loadings, the grouped and pooled fits recovered the target in 10 of 10 and 9 of 10 datasets, with mean false-active counts 0.4 and 0.1. All 120 fits across the four cells of the informative scenario converged. The comparison did not establish a separation between the prior configurations. The grouped path corrects loading KL to the returned prior, while the historical pooled path retains the incoming-prior KL. Absolute objective and stopping comparisons therefore do not isolate prior grouping. The matched TCGA analysis below is **not validated by simulation**.

The descriptive TCGA comparison used 144 patients with matched expression, methylation and survival, including 75 deaths. It fit five programs using 2,218 genes and 10,000 CpGs, with the same folds and training-only scaling. In one run of five-fold CV, mean concordance was 0.591 for expression, 0.545 for methylation, 0.531 for the joint grouped-prior fit and 0.536 for the joint pooled-prior fit. The paired joint-minus-expression differences were −0.060 (SE 0.024) and −0.055 (SE 0.030), respectively. Of 24 fits, 21 converged and three expression folds reached the 300-sweep limit. These expression results use the capped fits and differ from the separately restarted, converged expression reference in @sec-week-methylation. No joint program met the descriptive rule for a loading pattern distinct from both single-modality fits. Methylation dominated score precision in some programs. No joint configuration was adopted.

The joint model is still in development, and Chapter 4 presents it as a proposed contribution. Its purpose is interpretive: to show which genes and CpG sites load on the same programs and whether some programs load on one data type only. It is not expected to predict much better than expression alone.

A third simulation planted an expression-only, a methylation-only and a joint program, with 50 genes, 50 CpG sites and 120 training patients. Separate loading priors found the right loading and data-type pattern more often than one pooled prior: in 5 against 1 of 10 datasets for the expression-only program, 2 against 0 for the methylation-only program and 7 against 5 for the joint program. No fit recovered all three programs in the same dataset. The methylation-only program had the smaller coefficient ($\beta = 0.35$) and was rarely found by either prior.

With five times as many CpG sites as genes, methylation dominated the shared scores. We tried to balance the two data types by raising each one's reconstruction likelihood to a power $w_m$, as $w_S$ does for the survival term. Down-weighting methylation by the feature-count ratio ($w = 0.2$) or by the ratio of leading eigenvalues emptied the methylation loadings in nearly every program. A path of fixed weights showed that the loss begins early. At $w = 0.7$ the methylation share of the prognostic program's score precision fell from 52% and 60% to 21% and 9% in the two simulation cells, 42 and 46 of 50 methylation loading blocks were empty, and no weight below 1 improved recovery. The weight lowers each site's evidence for its own loading by the same factor that it lowers methylation's influence on the scores, so empirical Bayes shrinks the methylation loadings to zero. On the matched TCGA patients at 10,000 sites, lowering the weight to 0.3 or below changed two programs from joint to expression-only, while the program with the largest methylation share stayed above 94% methylation at every weight. No program at any weight was distinct from both single-data-type fits.

The fixed full-data fits were scored once in 50 ICGC donors with matched expression and methylation and 30 deaths. Concordance was 0.660 for expression alone, 0.636 and 0.594 for methylation alone at 10,000 and 100,000 sites, and 0.692 for the unweighted joint fit. The joint-minus-expression difference was 0.032, with a 95% donor-bootstrap interval from −0.093 to 0.147. These scores are descriptive and chose nothing. The matched ICGC set overlaps the PACA-AU donors of the expression validation series and has been examined in earlier analyses (@sec-external-uses).

The multimodal work is paused. Two alternatives remain untested: weighting methylation only in the score update, and summarizing CpG sites, for example by genomic region, so that the feature counts are closer.

## Survival through the scores or through the projection {#sec-week-lb}

The working model links survival to the projection of the data on the loadings,
$\eta = (YF)\beta$, and scores new patients by that projection. The alternative links survival
to the latent scores, $\eta = L\beta$, and scores new patients by fold-in, which solves for
their scores under the stored priors. This comparison fits both on identical input, priors,
starting values and folds, so only the parameterization of the hazard differs. It reports
simulation recovery, training cross-validation, the programs of the two full fits and, as
description only, the external scores of the two fixed models. Below, the projection model is
the working YFB fit and the latent-score model is the fit with $\eta = L\beta$. Both use rank
`r tcv_K`, the 2,218-gene input with z-scores within cohort, point-Laplace priors on $L$ and
$F$, a Normal prior on $\beta$ and $w_S = 1$ on real data. The simulation uses $w_S = 1$ and
$w_S = 10$, the latter in the survival-block form of @sec-weight.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lb-sim
#| tbl-cap: "Latent-score model ($\\eta = L\\beta$, new patients by fold-in) and projection model ($\\eta = (YF)\\beta$) at rank 5 in simulation at 2,000 genes, ten datasets per cell. Entries give the latent-score model first and the projection model second. Recovered counts datasets. False-active is the mean number of survival-active programs per fit that match no planted program. Validation C is the mean over datasets with a defined concordance. The latent-score model gave constant validation risk scores, so an undefined concordance, in 4 datasets at the 0.05% share with w_S = 1 and in 2 with w_S = 10. Every fit converged."
k5s_tab <- unique(k5s[c("design", "share", "w_S")])
k5s_tab <- k5s_tab[order(k5s_tab$design == "S14_strong", k5s_tab$share, k5s_tab$w_S), ]
pr <- function(f, d = 1) mapply(function(de, s, w) {
  a <- k5s_cell(de, s, w, "LB"); b <- k5s_cell(de, s, w, "YFB"); paste(f(a, d), f(b, d), sep = " / ")
}, k5s_tab$design, k5s_tab$share, k5s_tab$w_S)
stopifnot(all(k5s$converged == k5s$expected_seeds),
          identical(as.integer(subset(k5s, design == "S14_strong" & model == "LB")$validation_C_defined[order(subset(k5s, design == "S14_strong" & model == "LB")$w_S)]), c(6L, 8L)),
          all(subset(k5s, model == "YFB" | design == "S9")$validation_C_defined == 10))
kable(data.frame(
  Cell = ifelse(k5s_tab$design == "S9", "Fixed-weight", "Near-threshold, strong survival"),
  `Planted share` = pct(k5s_tab$share, 2), `w_S` = k5s_tab$w_S,
  Recovered = pr(function(r, d) r$recovery_successes),
  `False-active` = pr(function(r, d) num(r$false_active_mean, d)),
  `Validation C` = pr(function(r, d) num(r$validation_C_mean, 3)),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lcccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lb-cv
#| tbl-cap: "Latent-score and projection models at rank 5 in five-fold training cross-validation. Concordance counts only pairs of patients from the same cohort. The latent-score model scores held-out patients by fold-in and the projection model by projection. The difference is projection minus latent-score, and its standard error is the standard deviation of the five fold differences divided by the square root of 5. Every fit and every fold-in converged."
stopifnot(all(k5_cv$converged), all(k5_cv$foldin_converged))
kable(rbind(
  data.frame(Fold = as.character(k5_y$fold), `Latent-score C` = num(k5_l$C_within),
             `Projection C` = num(k5_y$C_within), Difference = sgn(k5_y$C_within - k5_l$C_within),
             check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Fold = "Mean", `Latent-score C` = num(k5_cw$mean_LB), `Projection C` = num(k5_cw$mean_YFB),
             Difference = paste0(sgn(k5_cw$YFB_minus_LB), " (SE ", num(k5_cw$paired_SE), ")"),
             check.names = FALSE)), row.names = FALSE, align = "lccc")
```

**Result.** The projection model is kept. In the fixed-weight cells the two models recovered
the planted program equally often (@tbl-lb-sim). At $w_S = 1$ the latent-score model marked
more programs survival-active that matched no planted program, with means of
`r num(min(subset(k5s, design == "S9" & w_S == 1 & model == "LB")$false_active_mean), 1)` to
`r num(max(subset(k5s, design == "S9" & w_S == 1 & model == "LB")$false_active_mean), 1)` per fit
against `r num(min(subset(k5s, design == "S9" & w_S == 1 & model == "YFB")$false_active_mean), 1)`
to `r num(max(subset(k5s, design == "S9" & w_S == 1 & model == "YFB")$false_active_mean), 1)`
for the projection model. At $w_S = 10$ both models had at most
`r num(max(subset(k5s, design == "S9" & w_S == 10)$false_active_mean), 1)` per fit in those
cells. Near the detection threshold the latent-score model recovered the program in
`r k5s_cell("S14_strong", 5e-4, 1, "LB")$recovery_successes` and
`r k5s_cell("S14_strong", 5e-4, 10, "LB")$recovery_successes` of 10 datasets at the two weights
and the projection model in `r k5s_cell("S14_strong", 5e-4, 1, "YFB")$recovery_successes` and
`r k5s_cell("S14_strong", 5e-4, 10, "YFB")$recovery_successes`, and the projection model had
more false-active programs there. A third generator simulated survival from the latent scores
instead of the projection, with six datasets per cell. There the mean correlation between the
fitted and true survival scores on validation patients was
`r ci(min(subset(k5m, model == "LB")$matched_score_mean), max(subset(k5m, model == "LB")$matched_score_mean), 2)`
for the latent-score model and
`r ci(min(subset(k5m, model == "YFB")$matched_score_mean), max(subset(k5m, model == "YFB")$matched_score_mean), 2)`
for the projection model, and `r sum(k5m$expected_seeds - k5m$converged)` fits at $w_S = 10$
reached the 300-sweep cap. The simulation run also issued at least 50 R warnings whose messages
were not saved, so their source cannot be checked.

In training cross-validation the paired concordance difference was small (@tbl-lb-cv). Mean
within-cohort concordance was `r num(k5_cw$mean_LB)` for the latent-score model and
`r num(k5_cw$mean_YFB)` for the projection model, a paired difference of
`r sgn(k5_cw$YFB_minus_LB)` (SE `r num(k5_cw$paired_SE)`). The two full-data fits gave nearly the
same risk score, with fitted predictors correlated at `r num(k5_eta$eta_correlation)`.
Corresponding programs shared all 20 of their genes with the largest absolute loadings, and
non-corresponding programs shared none. Programs `r andj(k5_active)` were
survival-active in both full fits. Within each fit, $L_k$ and $(YF)_k$ correlated
`r num(min(k5_lyf$cor_L_YF))` to `r num(max(k5_lyf$cor_L_YF))`. Across the five folds the
latent-score model had `r min(k5_fold_act("LB"))` to `r max(k5_fold_act("LB"))` survival-active
programs (mean `r num(mean(k5_fold_act("LB")), 1)`) and the projection model
`r min(k5_fold_act("YFB"))` to `r max(k5_fold_act("YFB"))` (mean
`r num(mean(k5_fold_act("YFB")), 1)`). Scored once on the five external series, the two fixed
fits differed by less than 0.01 in every series (@tbl-external-k5). Their equal-series means were
`r num(kp("equal_LB")$estimate)` and `r num(kp("equal_YFB")$estimate)`, a paired difference of
`r sgn(kp("equal_diff")$estimate)` (95% donor-bootstrap interval
`r ci(kp("equal_diff")$lower, kp("equal_diff")$upper)`). With each series weighted by its
comparable pairs they were `r num(kp("pair_LB")$estimate)` and `r num(kp("pair_YFB")$estimate)`,
a difference of `r sgn(kp("pair_diff")$estimate)`
(`r ci(kp("pair_diff")$lower, kp("pair_diff")$upper)`).

The two models link survival to different quantities. In the latent-score model $L_k$ is the
posterior activity of program $k$ given the expression and the other programs. A new patient has
no fitted activity, so fold-in estimates it under the stored priors and noise precisions without
using survival. In the projection model the score of program $k$ is a weighted sum of the
patient's standardized gene levels, with the loadings as weights, and a new patient is scored
by that sum. Under the factor model $Y \approx LF^\top$ plus noise, so
$YF \approx L(F^\top F)$ plus noise. When the loadings are not orthogonal, $F^\top F$ has nonzero
off-diagonal entries, and the projection score of one program mixes in the latent activities of
the others. The within-fit correlations above show that this mixing was small here. The
coefficients also refer to different units. The latent-score coefficient is a log hazard ratio
per unit of latent activity, whose size depends on the scale of the loadings, and the projection
coefficient is a log hazard ratio per training standard deviation of the projection score, so
their hazard ratios cannot be compared directly.

We keep the projection model. The paired concordance differences in training and the external
series are reported above with their uncertainty. In simulation at $w_S = 1$ the latent-score model marked more programs survival-active
that matched no planted program in the three variance cells of the fixed-weight simulation,
though near the detection threshold the projection model marked more, and the projection model scores a new patient directly from
expression, without a fold-in fit.

## Training cross-validation of the gene screen, input scaling and rank {#sec-week-redo}

Three choices of the current model were set with external concordance (@sec-external-uses).
Each is redone here by five-fold training cross-validation, as described in @sec-rank. Two
outcome-free gene screens are compared: the current 2,218-gene screen and a variance screen
after quantile normalization. The input scalings compared are z-scores within cohort, division
by the within-cohort standard deviation, and a within-patient rank transform followed by
z-scores. The rank is selected over $K = 2, \dots, 12$ by the one-standard-error rule, with the
number of programs with nonzero loadings and of survival-active programs reported at each $K$.

**Result.** The current screen and the z-scores within cohort are kept, and training
cross-validation selects rank `r tcv_K`. No alternative screen or scaling was better than the current input in
within-cohort concordance. Concordance was flat from $K = `r tcv_K`$ to `r max(tcv_k$K)` and
lower below $K = `r tcv_K`$, and the one-standard-error rule selected $K = `r tcv_K`$
(@sec-results-rank). The working model uses $K = `r tcv_K`$, which the rule also selected when the
cross-validation was repeated over five random partitions of the patients. At that rank the
point-exponential prior on expression divided by its within-cohort standard deviation still
loses to the point-Laplace prior ([Appendix D](#sec-appendix-d)).

## External scoring of the fixed working model {#sec-week-external}

The supervised YFB fit ($w_S = 1$, 2,218 genes, rank `r tcv_K`) was fixed on training data and then scored once on the
five external series, as part of the comparison of the two survival links. Its concordance by
series and its pooled means are in @sec-working-model. Its comparison with the two-step fit,
calibration slopes, hazard ratios, risk groups and comparator differences are in
@sec-results-fair and @sec-results-comparators.

# Results {#sec-results}

## The working model at rank 5 {#sec-working-model}

On the `r train_n[["TCGA_PAAD"]] + train_n[["CPTAC"]]` training patients, the supervised YFB fit
($w_S = 1$, 2,218 genes, rank `r tcv_K`) had mean within-cohort cross-validated concordance
`r num(k5_cw$mean_YFB)` (SE `r num(k5_se_y)` over the folds of the parameterization comparison), and all five fold fits converged
(@tbl-lb-cv). The fit to all training patients converged after
`r k5_fullm$n_iter` sweeps. Programs
`r andj(k5_active)` were survival-active (@tbl-programs-k5). Program
`r k5_full$program[which.min(k5_full$beta)]` was protective, and the others were adverse. Program
3 had an adverse coefficient below the 1.96 threshold, and Program 1 had a coefficient of essentially zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-programs-k5
#| tbl-cap: "Survival coefficients of the supervised YFB fit (w_S = 1, 2,218 genes, rank 5) to all training patients. Coefficients are log hazard ratios per training SD of the program score, with posterior SDs. z is the coefficient divided by its posterior SD. Survival-active: |z| at least 1.96. Each program matches the rank-7 program with the same number (@sec-model-states)."
kable(data.frame(Program = k5_full$program,
  `Coefficient (SD)` = paste0(num(k5_full$beta), " (", num(k5_full$beta_sd), ")"),
  z = num(k5_full$z, 1), `Hazard ratio per SD` = num(k5_full$hazard_ratio, 2),
  `Survival-active` = ifelse(k5_full$survival_active, "yes", "no"),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "ccccc")
```

Scored once on the five external series, the fixed fit had concordance from
`r num(min(k5_ey$C))` in `r cohort_label[[k5_ey$cohort[which.min(k5_ey$C)]]]` to
`r num(max(k5_ey$C))` in `r cohort_label[[k5_ey$cohort[which.max(k5_ey$C)]]]`
(@tbl-external-k5). The equal-series mean was `r num(kp("equal_YFB")$estimate)` (95%
donor-bootstrap interval `r ci(kp("equal_YFB")$lower, kp("equal_YFB")$upper)`), and the mean
weighted by comparable pairs within series was `r num(kp("pair_YFB")$estimate)`
(`r ci(kp("pair_YFB")$lower, kp("pair_YFB")$upper)`). The donor bootstrap keeps all records of a
PACA-AU donor together across the two PACA-AU series.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-external-k5
#| tbl-cap: "External concordance of the supervised YFB fit (w_S = 1, 2,218 genes, rank 5) and of the latent-score model fitted on the same input (@sec-week-lb). Each series was scored once. Series intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals over records. The difference is projection minus latent-score on the same resamples. Pooled rows give the equal-series mean and the mean weighted by comparable pairs, with 95% donor-bootstrap intervals. Calibration slopes of the working model are in @tbl-external."
k5_row <- function(lab, a, b, d) data.frame(Series = lab, `C, working model (95% CI)` = a,
  `C, latent-score model (95% CI)` = b, `Difference (95% CI)` = d, check.names = FALSE)
pc <- function(m) paste0(num(kp(m)$estimate), " (", ci(kp(m)$lower, kp(m)$upper), ")")
pcd <- function(m) paste0(sgn(kp(m)$estimate), " (", ci(kp(m)$lower, kp(m)$upper), ")")
kable(rbind(
  k5_row(unname(cohort_label[k5_ey$cohort]),
         paste0(num(k5_ey$C), " (", ci(k5_ey$lower, k5_ey$upper), ")"),
         paste0(num(k5_el$C), " (", ci(k5_el$lower, k5_el$upper), ")"),
         paste0(sgn(k5_ed$difference), " (", ci(k5_ed$lower, k5_ed$upper), ")")),
  k5_row("Equal-series mean", pc("equal_YFB"), pc("equal_LB"), pcd("equal_diff")),
  k5_row("Comparable-pair weighted", pc("pair_YFB"), pc("pair_LB"), pcd("pair_diff"))),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lccc")
```

## Supervised fit against the two-step fit {#sec-results-fair}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cv
#| tbl-cap: "Five-fold training cross-validation on the 2,218-gene set (single log). Both fits have rank 5 and use the same folds. The two-step fit takes the loadings of the $w_S = 0$ fit and fits a Cox model on the training program scores. C is Harrell's concordance index over all pairs in each held-out fold, with z-scores computed once on all 273 patients. This differs from the within-cohort concordance with fold-specific scaling of @tbl-lb-cv, which gives the working model 0.655. Survival-active: coefficient at least 1.96 posterior standard deviations from zero in the fit to all training patients (Wald test for the two-step fit). Convergence refers to the factorization. SE is standard error across folds. Model: supervised YFB fit (w_S = 1, 2,218 genes, rank 5) and its two-step comparator."
cvt <- data.frame(
  Fit = c("Supervised, w_S = 1", "Two-step (w_S = 0 loadings, then Cox)"),
  `Mean fold C (SE)` = c(paste0(num(cv_w1$mean_C), " (", num(cv_w1$se_C), ")"),
                         paste0(num(cv_ts$mean_C), " (", num(cv_ts$se_C), ")")),
  `Pooled out-of-fold C` = num(c(cv_w1$pooled_oof_C, cv_ts$pooled_oof_C)),
  `CV partial log-likelihood` = num(c(cv_w1$cv_partial_loglik, cv_ts$cv_partial_loglik), 1),
  `Folds converged` = paste0(c(cv_w1$folds_converged, cv_ts$folds_converged), " of ", nrow(ff)),
  `Survival-active` = c(cv_w1$full_active, cv_ts$full_active), check.names = FALSE)
kable(cvt, row.names = FALSE)
```

On the training patients the supervised fit had mean fold concordance `r num(cv_w1$mean_C)`
against `r num(cv_ts$mean_C)` for the two-step fit (@tbl-cv). The paired fold difference was
`r sgn(cv_diff)` (SE `r num(cv_diff_se)`). Every fold fit of both arms converged, the slowest after
`r max(ff_iter)` of 300 sweeps.

This configuration ($w_S = 1$, the 2,218-gene set, no survival screen) was fixed on training
data before any external cohort was scored with it. It was then scored once on the five external
series together with its two-step comparator (@tbl-external).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-external
#| tbl-cap: "External concordance of the fixed supervised fit and the two-step fit. Each series was scored once, after the configuration was fixed by training cross-validation. C intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals over patients. The difference is supervised minus two-step on the same resamples. The pooled comparison reports intervals from resampling records and resampling donors, plus a sensitivity excluding PACA-AU RNA-seq. The calibration slope is the coefficient of a Cox regression of held-out survival on the fitted risk score. A slope of 1 means the training coefficients predict hazard differences of the observed size. Model: supervised YFB fit (w_S = 1, 2,218 genes, rank 5) and its two-step comparator."
ord <- match(e_w1$cohort, e_ts$cohort)
xt <- data.frame(
  Series = cohort_label[e_w1$cohort],
  `C, supervised (95% CI)` = paste0(num(e_w1$C), " (", ci(e_w1$lo, e_w1$hi), ")"),
  `C, two-step` = num(e_ts$C[ord]),
  `Difference (95% CI)` = paste0(sgn(extd$diff[match(e_w1$cohort, extd$cohort)]), " (",
    ci(extd$lo[match(e_w1$cohort, extd$cohort)], extd$hi[match(e_w1$cohort, extd$cohort)]), ")"),
  `Slope, supervised` = num(e_w1$cal_slope, 2),
  `Slope, two-step` = num(e_ts$cal_slope[ord], 2), check.names = FALSE)
xt <- rbind(xt,
  data.frame(Series = "Mean of five series", `C, supervised (95% CI)` = num(mean(e_w1$C)),
             `C, two-step` = num(mean(e_ts$C)), `Difference (95% CI)` = "",
             `Slope, supervised` = "", `Slope, two-step` = "", check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Series = "Pooled, record bootstrap", `C, supervised (95% CI)` = "", `C, two-step` = "",
             `Difference (95% CI)` = paste0(sgn(pool5$diff), " (", ci(pool5$lo, pool5$hi), ")"),
             `Slope, supervised` = "", `Slope, two-step` = "", check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Series = "Pooled, donor bootstrap", `C, supervised (95% CI)` = "", `C, two-step` = "",
             `Difference (95% CI)` = paste0(sgn(pool_donor$diff), " (",
               ci(pool_donor$lo, pool_donor$hi), ")"),
             `Slope, supervised` = "", `Slope, two-step` = "", check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(Series = "Pooled, without PACA-AU RNA-seq", `C, supervised (95% CI)` = "",
             `C, two-step` = "",
             `Difference (95% CI)` = paste0(sgn(poolns$diff), " (", ci(poolns$lo, poolns$hi), ")"),
             `Slope, supervised` = "", `Slope, two-step` = "", check.names = FALSE))
kable(xt, row.names = FALSE)
```

The two fits had nearly the same concordance in every series, with series differences from
`r sgn(min(extd$diff[!grepl("pooled", extd$cohort)]))` to
`r sgn(max(extd$diff[!grepl("pooled", extd$cohort)]))`. Their mean external concordances were
`r num(mean(e_w1$C))` and `r num(mean(e_ts$C))`. The pooled paired difference was
`r sgn(pool5$diff)` (95% interval `r ci(pool5$lo, pool5$hi)`), and `r sgn(poolns$diff)`
(`r ci(poolns$lo, poolns$hi)`) without the PACA-AU RNA-seq series. The donor bootstrap interval
is `r ci(pool_donor$lo, pool_donor$hi)` for the full panel. Moffitt and Dijk were the weakest
series for both fits.

The supervised slope was closer to one in `r sum(calibration_closer)` of `r nrow(e_w1)`
series, but the two fits' slopes differed by at most `r num(max(cal_gap), 2)`, less than the
slope standard error in every series (`r ci(cal_se_rng[1], cal_se_rng[2], 2)`,
@tbl-comparator-series). The two-step slope was closer to one in
`r andj(unname(cohort_label[e_w1$cohort[!calibration_closer]]))`. In PACA-AU RNA-seq the
supervised slope was `r num(e_w1$cal_slope[e_w1$cohort == "PACA_AU_seq"], 2)`, compared with
`r num(e_ts$cal_slope[e_ts$cohort == "PACA_AU_seq"], 2)` for two-step. In Puleo it
was `r num(e_w1$cal_slope[e_w1$cohort == "Puleo_array"], 2)` against
`r num(e_ts$cal_slope[e_ts$cohort == "Puleo_array"], 2)`.

As a
summary on the scale DeSurv reports [@Young2026], the hazard ratio per standard deviation of the
risk score, from a Cox model stratified by series over all `r big(exth$n[1])` records, was
`r num(exth$hr_per_sd[exth$model == "w1"], 2)` (95% donor-clustered CI
`r ci(exth_donor$donor_lo[exth$model == "w1"], exth_donor$donor_hi[exth$model == "w1"], 2)`) for the supervised fit and
`r num(exth$hr_per_sd[exth$model == "twostep"], 2)`
(`r ci(exth_donor$donor_lo[exth$model == "twostep"], exth_donor$donor_hi[exth$model == "twostep"], 2)`) for the two-step
fit. The intervals are clustered on donor because the two PACA-AU series share donors, as in
@tbl-comparators.

## What survival does to the real-data loadings {#sec-results-loadings}

On the training data at $w_S = 1$, survival supplies between
`r sci(share_rng[1])` and `r sci(share_rng[2])` of the loading precision (median over
programs, across the gene-set sizes below). The simulation cell medians at the same weight ranged from `r num(min(tapply(s9_fixed_share$share_match, s9_fixed_share$variance, median)), 2)` to `r num(max(tapply(s9_fixed_share$share_match, s9_fixed_share$variance, median)), 2)` at the larger gene count. Two things keep it small on real data. The fitted coefficients are small
(largest $|\bar\beta_k|$ `r num(full_w1$max_abs_beta, 2)` per standard deviation of the program
score), and the share scales with $E[\beta_k^2]$. The real programs also explain much more
expression variance than the planted programs in simulation, so their expression precision is
large. The loading correlations between the fits round to `r num(min(matched_loadings$abs_r))` for every matched pair. The paired concordance difference is reported in @sec-results-fair.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-size
#| tbl-cap: "Training cross-validation by input gene-set size. Sets are nested and outcome-free, ranked by the per-cohort mean and variance rank. The 2,218-gene set is the default. C counts all pairs in each held-out fold, as in @tbl-cv. Match: absolute loading correlation of the one survival-active program of the all-genes supervised fit with its best match at each size. Model: supervised YFB fit (w_S = 1, 2,218 genes, rank 5) and its two-step comparator."
w <- sizes[sizes$arm == "w1", ]; t2 <- sizes[sizes$arm == "w0cox", ]
ag <- s11_agree[s11_agree$arm == "w1", ]
stopifnot(all(ag$ref_active == 1), all(w$folds_converged == 5), all(t2$folds_converged == 5))
st <- data.frame(Genes = big(w$n_genes),
  `Supervised C (SE)` = paste0(num(w$mean_C), " (", num(w$se_C), ")"),
  `Two-step C (SE)` = paste0(num(t2$mean_C[match(w$set, t2$set)]), " (", num(t2$se_C[match(w$set, t2$set)]), ")"),
  `Folds converged, supervised` = w$folds_converged,
  Match = ag$matches[match(w$set, ag$set)], check.names = FALSE)
kable(st, row.names = FALSE)
# Sizes up to about 8,000 genes form the flat part of the curve.
flat <- w$n_genes <= 8001; flat_t <- t2$n_genes <= 8001
scr_w1 <- s11_scr[s11_scr$arm == "w1", ]
scr_w1 <- scr_w1[order(scr_w1$N), ]
stopifnot(nrow(scr_w1) == 3, max(scr_w1$C_S) < cv_w1$mean_C)
```

Adding genes beyond the 2,218-gene set did not help either fit (@tbl-size, @fig-feature-size).
The curve was flat up to about 8,000 genes, with supervised concordance from
`r num(min(w$mean_C[flat]))` to `r num(max(w$mean_C[flat]))` and two-step concordance from
`r num(min(t2$mean_C[flat_t]))` to `r num(max(t2$mean_C[flat_t]))`. At the two largest sets the
concordance of both fits was `r ci(min(w$mean_C[!flat], t2$mean_C[!flat_t]), max(w$mean_C[!flat], t2$mean_C[!flat_t]))`. Every size lay within about one standard error of the others, and
every fold fit converged. The two arms tracked each other at every size, so the gene count does
not change the comparison of @sec-results-fair. The curve does not single out one size, and the
2,218-gene screen is kept on the paired screen comparison of @sec-results-rank.

Screening genes on survival inside each training fold, by a cohort-stratified univariable Cox
test, gave the supervised fit gains of `r andj(sgn(scr_w1$diff_S_minus_U))` over an outcome-free
screen of `r andj(big(scr_w1$N))` genes. Each was within
`r num(max(scr_w1$diff_S_minus_U / scr_w1$diff_se), 1)` paired standard errors, and no screened set
beat the supervised fit on all 2,218 genes (best `r num(max(scr_w1$C_S))`). With survival
permuted in simulated data, the $w_S = 1$ fit at rank 7 had
`r num(min(s11_null$n_active), 1)` to `r num(max(s11_null$n_active), 1)` false-active programs per
dataset on average.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Cross-validated training concordance by gene-set size. Points give fold means with one standard error. Model: supervised YFB fit (w_S = 1, 2,218 genes, rank 5) and its two-step comparator."
#| out-width: "100%"
chapter_figure("sup_real_size_curve_k5")
```

## Simulation: supervision strength and the weight choice {#sec-results-weight}

The simulations in this section and the next fit rank 7. In the fixed-weight simulation at
$w_S = 1$ with `r big(s9_large_p)` genes the fit recovered the planted program in all `r unique(subset(s9_cv, p == s9_large_p)$n)` datasets per variance cell, with
mean false-active counts `r paste(num(s9_w1_2k$mean_false_active, 1), collapse = ", ")`, and every
fit converged. No fit at a weight of `r min(s9_nonconvergent$w_S)` or greater converged at the larger gene count. Training CV selected the unit weight in `r sum(s9_choices$arm == "w1")` of `r sum(s9_cv$n)` datasets. The
coefficients at $w_S = 1$ were attenuated: median validation calibration slopes were
`r paste(num(s9_slopes$cal_slope_exact, 2), collapse = ", ")` across the three cells, where one denotes calibration. Mean validation concordance ranged from `r ci(min(s9_w1_2k$c_validation_mean), max(s9_w1_2k$c_validation_mean))`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s13
#| tbl-cap: "Weight chosen by five-fold cross-validated partial log-likelihood (the cross-validated-weight simulation, rank 7), against the two-step fit on the same datasets. The share cells are the 2,000-gene cells of the fixed-weight simulation, labelled by planted variance share. The weaker-survival cell uses a smaller coefficient. Ten datasets per cell. Paired entries show supervised / two-step. False-active is the mean false-active count. C is mean validation concordance. Slope is the median calibration slope with exact event times."
x <- s13
arm_lab <- c(A1 = "Block-weighted", A2 = "Joint-posterior")
kable(data.frame(Fit = arm_lab[x$arm], Cell = c(weak = "Weaker survival", v0.0025 = "0.25% share", v0.01 = "1% share", v0.05 = "5% share")[x$cell], `Weights (count)` = x$weights,
  Recovered = paste(x$recovered, x$twostep_recovered, sep = " / "),
  `False-active` = paste(num(x$mean_false_active, 1), num(x$twostep_false_active, 1), sep = " / "),
  C = paste(num(x$c_validation), num(x$twostep_c), sep = " / "),
  Slope = paste(num(x$slope_median, 2), num(x$twostep_slope, 2), sep = " / "),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

In the cross-validated-weight simulation the weights selected by partial log-likelihood increased with the planted signal
(@tbl-s13). Both supervised arms and the matched two-step fit recovered the planted program
in every dataset. Mean validation concordance differed by at most
`r num(max(abs(s13$c_validation - s13$twostep_c)))`. Each arm had a median calibration slope between 0.8 and 1.25 in
`r unique(s13v$slope_cells)` of `r unique(s13v$gate_cells)` variance cells, so the coefficients stayed attenuated. The mean-field
arm's largest mean null false-active count at its modal weight was
`r num(s13v$null_max_false_active[s13v$arm == "A1"], 1)`.
The mean concordance of the joint and mean-field coefficient variants differed by at most
`r num(max(abs(s13_joint_delta$c_validation.x - s13_joint_delta$c_validation.y)))`.
